source.title: Scaling Laws Are Unreliable for Downstream Tasks: A Reality Check
source.authors: Nicholas Lourie; Michael Y Hu; Kyunghyun Cho

record.tranche_reason: The study conceptually tests downstream predictability and its sensitivity to experimental setup by reanalyzing existing model results and comparing scaling behavior across studies; it does not reproduce pretraining loss scaling measurements.
record.gate_note: Included the study's own reanalysis and evaluation results. Background statements and results attributed only to cited works are not recorded as rows. Individual task-level plot values and category assignments are not readable in the supplied text, so only the aggregate task counts and outcomes described in prose are recorded.
record.test_reason: A meta-analysis of existing downstream results, using Gadre et al. 2025 data and Magnusson et al. 2025 checkpoints the authors re-evaluated on C4. It argues that downstream predictability from pretraining loss (V6) holds in only 39% of tasks and depends on setup. It does not fit pretraining-loss laws.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors find predictable downstream scaling in only 39% of cases and say setup changes can qualitatively alter it, so investigators must verify scaling laws in their own settings.
record.recipe_differences: This is a reanalysis and cross-study comparison of downstream performance against validation loss, rather than a measurement of pretraining loss scaling with model size, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported downstream trends change with validation corpus, task, and experimental setup, including architecture details, prompt and shot choices, task format, and number of answer choices.

fits_no_version.finding: Which pretraining corpus looks better at a given validation loss flips with the choice of validation corpus and task. Qualitative downstream scaling behaviour also changes with the evaluation harness (shots, answer choices, format).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The mapping from pretraining loss to downstream performance depends on the validation corpus, pretraining data and evaluation setup, so downstream scaling laws are setup-specific.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The study relies on data and checkpoints from existing projects and notes possible biases shared between them. Its scaling-behavior categories are defined informally. The supplied text provides plot captions but not readable individual plotted values or all task-by-task category assignments.
record.rows_left_out: Individual task plots and assignments from Figures 5–10, and additional plotted comparisons in Figures 11–12, were not separately extracted because their task labels and point values are not readable in the supplied text; the explicit aggregate count and prose-described comparisons are included.

untested.parts: All of it: pretraining loss versus N, D or C.
All of it: no pretraining-loss extrapolation.
All of it. Architecture differences between setups are confounded with harness differences.
Downstream performance directly against parameters, tokens or compute. Quantitative extrapolation error to larger models.
Pretraining-law exponents and the compute-optimal split under different fitting or setup choices. Bending of loss curves.

record.verdict_notes: V7 links were dropped: the study's setup-sensitivity concerns downstream-vs-loss trends, not pretraining exponents or the compute split. The classification categories are informal and qualitative; R² values are only in the figures. SIQA was excluded because of a label bug. Neither data source is an original source of the claim.

versions.untested_parts: Pretraining held-out loss scaling with parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger-run pretraining losses from fits to smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations and their growth with compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities and training regimes, including repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer.
The paper examines downstream performance against validation loss and does not test downstream performance scaling directly against parameter count, training tokens, or compute.

The paper tests setup sensitivity and departures from predictable downstream scaling, but not pretraining-law exponents, compute-optimal allocations, or their dependence on parameter counting and training schedules.

rows.check: The 28 tasks show no predictable improvement (some are inverse, i.e. reversed). For V6 this is absence, not partial.

rows.subject: Gadre et al. (2025) models

rows.value: The scaling laws for C4 and RedPajama pretraining produce the same trend.
rows.note: The text says the curves superimpose under this validation-corpus choice.
rows.check: V7 removed. V7 concerns pretraining-law exponents and the compute-optimal split, not downstream trends.

rows.subject: Gadre et al. (2025) models
rows.operation_detail: Compared downstream scaling for C4 and RedPajama pretraining corpora using 100 Programming Languages validation data.
rows.measure: Downstream performance relative to validation loss
rows.value: C4 appears to achieve much better performance even for a worse validation loss.
rows.note: The study reports that changing validation data separates the scaling laws that previously superimposed.
rows.check: V7 removed. Loss on 100 PLs does not map the two corpora to one downstream curve.

rows.note: The text describes the relative trend between the two pretraining corpora.

rows.subject: Gadre et al. (2025) models
rows.operation_detail: Compared downstream scaling for C4 and RedPajama pretraining corpora using 100 Programming Languages validation data.
rows.measure: Relative downstream performance as scaling proceeds
rows.value: The relationship between the C4 and RedPajama scaling trends reverses again.
rows.note: The paper does not state the specific relative winner for this condition in prose.
rows.check: V7 removed. 'Reversed' described a flip in corpus ranking, not a reversal of downstream improvement with loss. The baseline should be the CoQA/C4-validation ranking.

rows.subject: Gadre et al. (2025) models

rows.note: The paper reports a positive trend but emphasizes differences in noisiness and shape across setups.
rows.check: V7 removed. The trend is positive but its shape and noise depend on setup. The text does not say which setup is noisier.

tranche.reason: The study supplies counterexamples to general downstream predictability and argues that V6 needs qualifications concerning task, corpora and experimental setup.

source_check.notes: The 39% figure describes this Gadre task set, not downstream tasks generally; Appendix C uses informal qualitative categories. The paper does not establish numerical extrapolation accuracy, and Gadre BoolQ is described as a clearer trend rather than explicitly a clean scaling law.
